raw_response:
Yes. **PlantUML's Salt is the first option I would try** for the workflow you describe: a compact text description becomes a screen wireframe, much as Mermaid turns text into a diagram.

1. **[PlantUML Salt](https://plantuml.com/salt)** — Salt has short notation for buttons, text fields, checkboxes, radio controls and dropdowns. Braces define layout groups and vertical bars divide columns, so a small form requires only a few lines. This is especially suitable for dialogs and straightforward screen layouts. Its output is schematic; the point is to communicate controls and structure rather than produce a finished interface. The [official version 1.2023.11 guide](https://pdf.plantuml.net/1.2023.11/PlantUML_Language_Reference_Guide_en.pdf) establishes that wireframe support predates November 2026. genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn182837744view0","turn182837744view1"]}}

2. **[Wiremark](https://github.com/Blackburn-Labs/wiremark)** — A particularly close fit if you want wireframes embedded in Markdown. You write a hierarchy of familiar component names, with indentation specifying containment. Defaults supply layout details, and the renderer produces a sketch-style SVG. It also supports named frames and links between them. The practical caveat is that you need its renderer or a compatible Markdown adapter; a custom fenced block does not acquire rendering support merely by being in a Markdown file. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn569975232view0"}}

3. **[Wireloom](https://github.com/StardockCorp/Wireloom)** — Another direct text-to-wireframe language, using indented descriptions such as a window containing panels, inputs and buttons. It produces self-contained SVG, which is useful for keeping the editable source beside a specification and including the rendered mockup wherever images are accepted. It also documents annotations and a wider set of UI controls. Choose this for compact screen descriptions; expect deliberately rough wireframes rather than pixel-perfect output. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn569975232view1"}}

4. **[WireScript](https://wirescript.org/)** — Uses Lisp-style nested expressions to describe screens, layout boxes and components. Its documentation shows a login form expressed entirely in text, reusable layout/component definitions, editor preview support and a CLI with HTML/PNG export. This is worth comparing if you are comfortable with parentheses and want reusable screen structures. Check the particular integration you need: the site lists the Obsidian plugin as coming soon. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn889349822view2"}}

5. **[WireDSL](https://github.com/Wire-DSL/wire-dsl)** — Provides a dedicated .wire language with project, screen, layout and component declarations, plus a browser preview and command-line rendering. The project documents SVG, PNG and PDF exports. It offers a more explicit structure for layouts and settings, which could suit larger screen specifications, although the syntax is heavier than Salt for a tiny form. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn569975232view2"}}

6. **[Mockdown, the ASCII-to-HTML implementation](https://github.com/sminnee/mockdown)** — A different approach: arrange input fields, checkboxes, radios and buttons in a fixed-width text document, then have the PHP implementation interpret that notation as an HTML mockup. This can be convenient if you like seeing the approximate arrangement directly in your source. It requires manual text alignment, however, and its repository has been archived since February 2024, so treat it as a legacy option whose setup may need attention. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn182837744view3"}}

My suggested starting comparison is **Salt for short forms and conventional dialogs**, then **Wiremark or Wireloom for a Markdown-centered workflow**. That recommendation is based on the documented syntax and output, not a benchmark of how quickly you personally will work.

I inspected these projects' public documentation, but did not install or execute them. For Wiremark, Wireloom, WireScript and WireDSL, the opened pages are current live documentation and I did not verify a dated version available by November 7, 2026; their historical availability remains unknown.
